title: Event Triggered Execution: Netsh Helper DLL
shortTitle: Event Triggered Execution: Netsh Helper DLL
summary: Netsh is the command line utility Windows uses to inspect and change network configuration, and it is extensible: it loads helper dynamic link libraries that add functionality. The list of helper libraries is stored in the registry under the Netsh key in the local machine software hive, which means registering a helper is a registry change rather than a file placed in a startup folder. Once registered, the helper library is loaded by netsh.exe, so the attacker's code executes inside a signed Microsoft process every time that utility runs. That trigger is unreliable for an attacker who cannot make netsh run, which is what makes this sub-technique a chaining technique: it is frequently paired with another persistence method, a scheduled task, or a piece of legitimate software such as a virtual private network client that calls netsh during its normal work. The execution context is whatever account launched netsh, so a helper alone usually inherits the caller's rights; combined with a high-privileged caller it can also escalate. Detection is straightforward when registry monitoring covers the Netsh key and process telemetry records netsh.exe loading a library from an unexpected, unsigned, or user-writable location, because the set of legitimate helpers is small and stable.

beginner.definition: Netsh is a built-in Windows command line tool for checking and changing network settings. It can load extra pieces of code, called helper libraries, to gain more features. This technique is when an attacker registers their own helper so it loads whenever the tool runs.
beginner.whyItMatters: The helper library runs inside a trusted Windows program, so it looks official. It is registered in the registry, so it stays in place across restarts. Some network software runs this tool automatically, which means the code can start on its own. It is often used together with another trick to make the code run more often.
howItWorks: The attacker places a library file on the disk of the victim machine.
They add the path of that library to the Windows registry key that lists the helper files.
Netsh reads that list each time it starts, so it loads the attacker's library automatically.
The library's startup code runs inside the trusted netsh process, which hides its true origin.
Because netsh does not always run on its own, the attacker often adds a second trigger elsewhere.
Network software such as a virtual private network client can call netsh and wake the payload.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel with a maintenance manual that says which tools to pick up before each repair job. Someone adds one tool to the list, kept in their own locker. The repair staff collect it every time they follow the manual, without asking why. The manual is official, so the locker is opened again and again.
takeaways: Netsh loads helper libraries that are listed in the registry, and that list can be abused.
The payload runs inside a signed Microsoft tool, so the parent process looks trustworthy.
Review the registered helper paths and check whether each library is signed and expected.

objectives: Explain what the netsh utility is used for on Windows.
Explain why netsh supports helper libraries and where they are registered.
Explain how a helper library executes when the utility runs.
Explain why this method is usually chained with another trigger.
Identify the registry and process evidence that reveals a malicious helper.
